svg.title: The EU trust architecture behind a qualified signature
svg.desc: A chain from the European Commission's list of trusted lists, through national trusted lists and qualified trust service providers, down to the signer's certificate and the signature in the document. Side notes explain what each link proves and how a validator walks the chain upward.
svg.text: Who vouches for whom: the trust chain behind a qualified signature
Trust is not built into the document. It is established link by link, and every link is a signed statement that can be checked.

g.text: THE CHAIN, TOP DOWN
European Commission: list of trusted lists (LOTL)
One XML file pointing to every national list. Signed with keys whose
certificates are published in the Official Journal of the EU.
National trusted list, one per member state
Kept by the national supervisory body. Lists each provider and each
service with its type, status (granted/withdrawn) and status history.
Qualified trust service provider (QTSP)
Audited by a conformity assessment body, supervised nationally. Its services:
qualified certificates
qualified timestamps
qualified validation, preservation
Certificate authority (CA) of the provider
Its CA certificate is the entry on the trusted list. It issues the signer’s
certificate after identity checks and publishes CRL/OCSP revocation data.
The signer’s qualified certificate
Name, public key, QC statements, validity, pointers to revocation data.
The matching private key sits on a qualified device the signer controls.
The signature inside the PDF, over the document’s bytes
WHAT EACH LINK PROVES
That the national list is genuine.
The LOTL carries the signing certificate of every
national list; the validator keeps the LOTL keys as
its only built-in trust anchor.
That the provider is qualified, and since when.
Status history matters: a certificate issued while
the service was “granted” stays qualified even if
the service is withdrawn later.
That someone audited the provider.
Conformity assessment against ETSI EN 319 401/411,
repeated at least every 24 months, with incident
reporting duties to the supervisor.
That the chain is unbroken and current.
Each certificate is signed by the one above; CRL or
OCSP answers, themselves signed, say whether any
link has been revoked.
That this key belongs to this person.
Identity was verified before issue; the QC statements
say the key is on a qualified device, so nobody else
could have used it.
That these exact bytes were signed with that key.
Mathematics, not trust: see “tamper protection”.

svg.text: A validator walks the chain upward, from the signature to the LOTL. Standards: trusted lists ETSI TS 119 612; certificate profiles ETSI EN 319 412;
validation ETSI EN 319 102-1; qualification ETSI TS 119 615.
